nodes.title: Chapter 1: What is the point of Rhetoric?
nodes.description: Aristotle defines rhetoric as the counterpart of dialectic and argues that a systematic art of proof, not appeals to emotion, is its true business.

nodes.title: Chapter 2: Argumentation techniques
nodes.description: Rhetoric as the faculty of finding the available means of persuasion: moral character, emotion, and the argument itself, via example and enthymeme.

nodes.title: Chapter 3: Types of Rhetoric
nodes.description: The three kinds of rhetorical speech — deliberative, forensic, and epideictic — their proper times, and the distinct end each one argues toward.

nodes.title: Chapter 4: Topics of deliberative rhetoric
nodes.description: The five subjects the deliberative orator must be ready to advise on: ways and means, war and peace, defence, food supply, and legislation.

nodes.title: Chapter 5: What people care about
nodes.description: A working definition of happiness and its parts — birth, friends, wealth, honor, health, beauty, strength, and good fortune — for the deliberative orator.

nodes.title: Chapter 6: The greater good, and its components
nodes.description: Aristotle defines the good as what all things aim at, catalogs the things generally recognized as good, and lists arguments for doubtful goods.

nodes.title: Chapter 7: The Impact of actions and trade-offs
nodes.description: How to weigh one good against another: Aristotle's rules for comparing things by size, cause, scarcity, duration, and general opinion.

nodes.title: Chapter 8: Types of Governments
nodes.description: The four forms of government — democracy, oligarchy, aristocracy, monarchy — their ends, and why an orator must know them.

nodes.title: Chapter 9: Epideictic Rhetoric, praise and blame, virtue and vice
nodes.description: Aristotle defines virtue and the noble, then sets out the topics and amplification techniques used in epideictic praise and blame.

nodes.title: Chapter 10: Litigation: accusation and defense
nodes.description: The motives behind wrongdoing — chance, nature, compulsion, habit, reason, anger, and desire — as material for accusation and defense.

nodes.title: Chapter 11: Motive
nodes.description: Aristotle explains motive through what people find pleasant, laying the ground for why people commit wrongdoing.

nodes.title: Chapter 12: Intent
nodes.description: The frame of mind of wrongdoers and the circumstances and victims that make wrongdoing seem safe to attempt.

nodes.title: Chapter 13: Justice and Legislation
nodes.description: Aristotle classifies just and unjust acts under particular and general law, and defines equity.

nodes.title: Chapter 14: Severity of transgressions
nodes.description: How to argue that a wrong act is greater or lesser in degree, with the rhetorical grounds for each.

nodes.title: Chapter 15: Trial Proceedings
nodes.description: The five inartificial proofs of forensic oratory — laws, witnesses, contracts, torture, and oaths.

nodes.title: I: Purposes and Definitions of Rhetoric
nodes.description: Book I of Aristotle's Rhetoric — its purposes, the three species of rhetoric, and the topics orators build arguments from, across 15 chapters.

nodes.title: III: Stylistic Delivery and Arrangement Techniques
nodes.description: Book III of Aristotle's Rhetoric covers style, word choice, and speech arrangement. Out of scope for this showcase.

nodes.title: II: Persuasion techniques
nodes.description: Book II of Aristotle's Rhetoric covers ethos, pathos, and logos — the three means of persuasion. Out of scope for this showcase.

nodes.description: What the three books of Aristotle's Rhetoric cover, who translated this text, and how this docsite conversion came together.
